title: "The Jews" in John's Gospel
lead: John uses the Greek hoi Ioudaioi, "the Jews", about seventy times: sometimes for the Jewish people and their customs, sometimes for people of Judea, and often for the Jerusalem authorities who oppose Jesus. This page is a study of the word and how to read and translate it in each place; the later use of these passages against Jews is treated on the anti-Judaism page.

sections.b: Jesus, his disciples and John the Baptist are all Jews, and Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that "salvation comes from the Jews" (John 4:22). Yet John often uses "the Jews" for people who question or oppose Jesus, especially the authorities in Jerusalem (John 1:19; 5:16–18; 9:22). Scholars read this in several ways: as the Judean leaders, as Judeans as opposed to Galileans, as a symbol of the unbelieving world, or as the synagogue of John's own day, from which believers in Jesus were being expelled (John 9:22; 16:2). This site keeps the Greek word in the text and explains each use in notes.
